item.title: Chem at 10: Tanja Junkers
item.description: In this Q&A, Tanja Junkers discusses how her childhood fascination with polymer chemistry developed into a career driven by curiosity, collaboration, and openness. She emphasizes the importance of teamwork and enjoyment in good science and remarks on the exciting changes that AI, automation, and robotics will bring to chemical research and the way it is conducted in the future.

item.title: Chem at 10: Jie Wu
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

In his interview with Chem, Prof. Jie Wu reflects on a career shaped by curiosity, resilience, and molecular creativity. From his early inspiration in natural product synthesis to his advances in flow chemistry, automation, and sustainable synthesis, he emphasizes the importance of staying true to scientific curiosity while envisioning how artificial intelligence (AI)-guided tools for multistep automated synthesis could make the synthesis of complex molecules safer, faster, and more accessible.

item.title: Chem at 10: Hai-Bo Yang
item.description: Dr. Hai-Bo Yang is a supramolecular chemist and serves as a member of Chem’s advisory board. In this interview celebrating Chem’s 10th anniversary, Dr. Yang shares his educational journey, scientific experiences, mentoring philosophy, and perspectives on inspiring the next generation of scientists. He also reflects on his experience as an advisory board member, author, reviewer, and reader of Chem and discusses his views on the journal’s development and future impact.

item.title: Chem at 10: Sarbajit Banerjee
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Prof. Sarbajit Banerjee is an international leader and innovator in the design of electrochemical materials and technologies. In this interview with Chem, he discusses finding a path in science, the joys of discovery, striving for a sustainable future through reimagining our relationship with materials, and the importance of interdisciplinary thinking.

item.title: New reactivity enables stereochemical inheritance
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

A two-time Potential Energy author, Zhe Dong now reintroduces himself as an associate professor at the Southern University of Science and Technology. Since his initial publication in the inaugural volume of Chem, he has become an independent researcher whose specific projects have changed but whose passion for challenging organic chemistry has not.

item.title: Catalysis engineering at the forefront of the chemical and energy transition
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Jingxiu Xie shares her career journey from earning a PhD in the Netherlands to conducting postdoctoral research in Germany and Norway and then returning to the Netherlands, where she is now an associate professor at the University of Groningen. She highlights her group’s research in catalysis engineering across multiple scales—from catalysts to reactors to processes—and argues that heterogeneous catalysis must evolve beyond isolated materials research to become a critical enabler of chemical processes and technological innovation.

item.title: Designing molecular interfaces for stable hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

From passivation to resilient molecular contacts: this Potential Energy article traces the evolution of the author's understanding of perovskite surfaces from static defect passivation to controlling the dynamic molecular organization and operational evolution of interfaces. These insights guide the design of chemically and structurally robust contacts for efficient and durable perovsktie photovoltaics.

item.title: High-resolution AFM imaging: Real bond or artifact?
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

High-resolution atomic force microscopy (HR-AFM) with a carbon monoxide (CO)-functionalized tip resolves molecular structures with single-bond precision, yet the interpretation of its bond-like contrast remains debated. In Cell Reports Physical Science, Chen et al. combine HR-AFM measurements with theoretical simulations to establish practical criteria for distinguishing genuine bond- from apparent bond-like features across covalent-, ionic-, and hydrogen-bonded systems.

item.title: Exploration of new sites: Remote functionalization by entangled boracycle migration
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Reporting in Nature, Quan and co-workers show that a borinane ring can relocate along a carbon chain, moving two reaction sites in a correlated manner. The rearrangement achieves selective functionalization at internal carbons that are difficult to access by conventional migratory processes, extending the range of positions from which molecular diversity can be generated.

item.title: Advanced bottom-up synthetic chemistry expanding the MXene family
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Conventional top-down etching routes, limited by scarce precursors and metal dissolution, have long hindered the birth of semiconducting and magnetic MXenes. Now, in Nature, Fang and co-workers unveil an intercalation-driven bottom-up chemistry that hatches a new lanthanide MXene family endowed with tunable semiconducting and ferromagnetic states.

item.title: Knots by design: Turning a polymer entanglement into a topological synthon
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Knots form spontaneously in long polymers, yet their de novo synthesis with precise control over topology, backbone, and dispersity has remained elusive. In Nature Chemistry, Du et al. introduce a metal-templated knot as a versatile topological synthon that generates trefoil knots with controlled molecular weights and defined chemistries. Chemically matched sets of topoisomers enable systematic study of topology-property relationships.

item.title: Molecular recognition guides ionic liquid design for mild PET depolymerization
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Rational catalyst design for polymer depolymerization requires understanding how catalysts interact with polymer substrates. In a recent issue of Nature Sustainability, Yan et al. establish cooperative molecular recognition as a design principle for ionic liquids, enabling selective PET depolymerization at exceptionally mild temperatures.

item.title: Structure-activity relationships at catalyst-pollutant interfaces in redox water purification
item.description: Catalytic redox treatment can transform persistent pollutants, but rational design is limited by complex water chemistry and dynamic catalyst surfaces. This review introduces catalyst-pollutant interface structure-activity relationships as a framework that connects pollutant identity, catalyst structure, reaction pathways, and local microenvironments to guide more predictable interface design.

item.title: Origins of universality of copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition
item.description: Copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition is one of the most robust platforms to connect two molecules—utilized by scientists working across fields ranging from chemical biology to polymer topology—but its operational simplicity should not be mistaken for a naive and universal mechanism. This perspective analyzes the different catalyst identities in this click reaction and outlines a dynamic catalytic network of interconverting copper species, thereby providing a framework for more translatable and predictive copper-catalyzed click reactions.

item.title: One catalyst, two geometries: Iridium catalysis enables stereodivergent synthesis of chiral Z- and E-allylated isochromanones
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Alkene geometry strongly influences molecular structure and function, yet methods that provide stereodivergent access to both E- and Z-configured chiral building blocks remain rare. In an upcoming issue of Chem Catalysis, You and co-workers combine contra-thermodynamic alkene isomerization with iridium-catalyzed asymmetric allylic substitution to access either E- or Z-allylated 3-isochromanones with high regio- and enantioselectivity.

item.title: Molecular-scale engineering of sulfide solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries: Prospects and challenges
item.description: Organic molecular additives are transforming how sulfide solid electrolytes interact with electrodes and their environment. As interfacial stability increasingly limits battery performance, this review examines how molecules, polymers, and supramolecular assemblies tune interfacial behavior, revealing emerging structure-function relationships that can guide the design of safer, higher-performance all-solid-state batteries.

item.title: A CLEAN framework of photothermal evaporation-coupled catalysis
item.description: In this perspective, we introduce a concept of photothermal evaporation-coupled catalysis (PECC) for simultaneous sunlight-driven water purification and chemical upgrading and propose the cost-effectiveness, life-cycle sustainability, emerging system integration, AI-assisted design, and near-zero compatibility (CLEAN) paradigm to leverage the microscale principles of PECC and macroscale technoeconomic feasibility toward scalable, sustainable solar water-chemical factories.

item.title: Regulating transport processes in oxygen evolution catalyst layers for proton exchange membrane water electrolysis
item.description: Efficient proton exchange membrane water electrolysis requires more than highly active catalysts. It also depends on effective transport within the anode catalyst layer. This review highlights how catalyst architecture, ionomer engineering, hierarchical pore design, and interface engineering collectively regulate water delivery, oxygen removal, proton conduction, and electron transport, providing design principles for transport-efficient, ultralow-Ir oxygen evolution catalyst layers in acidic water electrolysis for sustainable hydrogen production.

item.title: Living polymers turn 70
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

The discovery of living polymers has shaped the field of organic polymer chemistry for the past 70 years. This Backstory recounts Prof. Michael Szwarc’s account of the discovery and reviews earlier work from the Schlenk, Ziegler, and Scott laboratories. This historical evidence suggests that each of these laboratories could have independently discovered living polymers approximately 40 years earlier.

item.title: Chem at 10: Jihye Park
item.description: At the University of Minnesota, Dr. Jihye Park runs a materials chemistry lab centered on metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and the untapped potential of organic linker design. In this interview with Chem, she reflects on her journey into MOF chemistry, what she has learned about mentoring students, and the value of embracing unexpected outcomes in research.

item.title: Chem at 10: Guangbin Dong
item.description: In this interview with Chem, Prof. Guangbin Dong describes the non-scientific conversations he enjoys, offers advice to young scientists, and shares key aspects of his approach to mentorship. He also presents his perspective on exciting developments in synthetic chemistry, the impact of AI on scholarly publishing, and his overall experience with Chem.

item.title: Chem at 10: Gabriela S. Schlau-Cohen
item.description: Gabriela S. Schlau-Cohen, PhD, the Haslam-Dewey Professor of Chemistry at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, was selected to participate in Chem’s 10th anniversary interview series because of her contributions to the journal in spectroscopy and photosynthetic light harvesting. In this Q&A, she discusses the teachers who inspired her, the importance of carving one’s own path, and the excitement of making unexpected discoveries.

item.title: Chem at 10: Junichiro Yamaguchi
item.description: In this interview with Chem, Junichiro Yamaguchi reflects on his unconventional journey to becoming an organic chemist, the mentors who inspired him, and the challenges he has faced throughout his career. He also discusses the importance of friendship and mentorship in science, his experiences with Chem, and his perspectives on research, education, community building, and sustaining a passion for science.

item.title: Nanotechnology to program biomolecular function
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Devleena Samanta is an assistant professor of chemistry at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), an associate member of the UT Austin Cancer Research Institute, and a member of the Texas Materials Institute. She received her PhD from Stanford University and completed postdoctoral training at Northwestern University. Her laboratory develops nanoscale tools that sense and program biomolecular function for use in diagnostics, therapeutics, and biocatalysis. She is a 2024 Packard Fellow for Science and Engineering and a 2026 Cottrell Scholar.

item.title: Trading an atom for another: A new playbook for heterocycle synthesis
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Yoonsu Park received his BS and PhD degrees in chemistry from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and completed his doctoral studies under the supervision of Prof. Sukbok Chang. He then pursued postdoctoral research with Prof. Paul J. Chirik at Princeton University, where he investigated visible light-driven catalysis and metalloradical reactivity. In 2022, he returned to KAIST to begin his independent career as an assistant professor in the Department of Chemistry and was promoted to associate professor in 2025. His research group focuses on developing sustainable catalysis such as single-atom skeletal editing reactions.

item.title: Reimagining amine chemistry
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Xiaheng Zhang is currently a research group leader at the Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, where he runs a program focused on transformations involving amines. His curiosity in amines began with the pursuit of a research philosophy from his PhD and postdoctoral trainings and developed into a series of related projects seeking to bring new reactivities to C–N bonds.

item.title: Atomic-scale interface enables ultra-low-potential HMF oxidation to FDCA
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

The selective electrooxidation of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) at low potentials has been a persistent challenge. In this issue of Chem Circularity, Chen and coworkers report a Pd100Pt0.6 catalyst with abundant Pd–O–Ptδ+ interface sites that effectively lowers the reaction potential of the HMF oxidation reaction and enhances FDCA selectivity.

item.title: Can polymer mechanochemistry stop a bullet?
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

In the current issue of Nature, Johnson, Nelson, and coworkers demonstrate that mechanophore crosslinks can dramatically enhance ballistic impact resistance. By selectively releasing network constraints during extreme deformation, force-triggered chemistry enables local plastic flow in thermosets, revealing mechanochemistry as a design principle for materials operating far from equilibrium.

item.title: Stereoretentive radical-radical alkyl-alkyl cross-coupling by Ni-catalysis
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Stereogenic C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation through catalytic radical-radical cross-coupling (RRCC) reactions relies heavily on stereoconvergent coupling of two alkyl precursors facilitated by chiral ligands or auxiliaries. In Science, Baran and coworkers developed a stereoretentive RRCC that directly couples two distinct transient alkyl radicals, derived from enantioenriched sulfonylhydrazides and achiral alkyl halides, in the presence of an achiral ligand, which enables the coupling of two alkyl radicals together with precise stereochemical control.

item.title: Recent applications of axially chiral skeletons in asymmetric catalysis
item.description: Axially chiral architectures have emerged as privileged platforms in asymmetric catalysis, serving effectively as both chiral ligands and organocatalysts. Their prominence primarily stems from three intrinsic attributes: skeletal diversity for modular structural variation, structural rigidity for conformational stability, and versatile tunability for fine-tuning electronic and steric properties. As ligands, they modulate metal reactivity and selectivity. As organocatalysts, they directly activate substrates via diverse interaction modes. These features collectively enable precise stereochemical control, making these scaffolds broadly applicable in the construction of enantiomerically enriched molecules with high efficiency.

item.title: Design and organocatalytic enantioselective assembly of axially chiral boracyclohexylidenes and chiral boraspiranes
Defining stability in metal-organic frameworks through rigorous characterization
item.description: MOFs are promising porous materials for energy, environmental, and industrial applications but only if they are stable under relevant conditions. Smoljan et al. present a tutorial-style perspective outlining rigorous, multi-technique characterization protocols for four major stability classes: thermal, chemical, mechanical, and radiation. Demonstrated across seven well-known MOFs, these protocols provide a practical roadmap toward standardized, comparable stability reporting.

item.title: Catalyst: When self-driving labs begin to reason
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are evolving from automated experimental engines into reasoning scientific partners. In agentic SDLs, artificial intelligence (AI) agents coordinate perception, planning, experimentation, analysis, and reflection across the research cycle. By making metadecisions, including what to measure, which models to trust, when to ask humans, and how to revise hypotheses, agentic SDLs move beyond closed-loop optimization toward adaptive, context-aware scientific discovery. This Catalysis article discusses how reasoning agents can expand autonomy, accelerate learning, and reshape scientific practice.

item.title: Reaction: Electrochemistry needs agentic AI that explains as well as optimizes
item.description: Self-driving laboratories can accelerate electrochemical discovery, but optimization alone is not enough. We argue that agentic artificial intelligence should recognize when objectives, models, or measurements are inadequate; explain anomalous results; propose competing hypotheses; and design discriminating experiments. But even with these capabilities, human scientists remain essential in identifying meaningful questions, evaluating explanations, setting research priorities, and ensuring accountability.

item.title: Reaction: The art of autonomous chemistry
item.description: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) promises self-driving laboratories (SDLs) capable of autonomous reasoning, yet general-purpose synthetic chemistry remains overwhelmingly manual. Automation still stumbles on ordinary tasks, remains costly and inaccessible, and offers too little relief to justify adoption. Moreover, poor FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) data practices leave AI models ill trained for chemistry. The authors call for democratized, modular hardware; rigorous FAIR data collection; and a Slurm-like workload manager distributing experiments across mature SDLs—freeing chemists to conceive questions rather than run columns.

item.title: Reaction: Navigating the path to reasoning laboratories
item.description: The convergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) and self-driving laboratories promises to move autonomous science beyond closed-loop optimization toward deliberate scientific reasoning. But this transition will not be a single leap. We argue that it runs through semi-autonomous laboratories, where AI agents and human scientists share cognitive and physical workloads. The more consequential question is not when full autonomy arrives but what we optimize for along the way and whether we build systems that narrow science or expand its scope.

item.title: Reaction: Building trust infrastructure for agentic experimental science beyond fragile eloquence
item.description: Agentic self-driving laboratories are transforming artificial intelligence (AI) from a mere experimental optimizer into a collaborator that hypothesizes, reasons, and adapts. To avoid becoming an “eloquent layer over brittle automation,” we must advocate for explainable reasoning, digital safety twins to counter the “curse of rarity,” safety-critic agents, verifiable agent-to-agent identity, and institutional governance. As autonomy expands, scientists shift from experimenters to stewards, a role sustained only by robust technical safeguards and a shared culture of safety.

item.title: Reaction: Self-driving labs need models of the chemical world
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Self-driving laboratories are moving from automated execution to scientific reasoning. This reaction argues that the next step requires experimentally grounded models of the chemical world. Such models connect laboratory actions, latent chemical states, observations, uncertainty, and updates. They allow agents to choose experiments that test beliefs and improve metrics. Building them will require machine-executable protocols, multimodal measurements, provenance, transferable representations, and human judgment so that autonomous laboratories can accumulate chemical understanding across instruments, campaigns, and sites over time more reliably.

item.title: High-entropy-inspired multi-principal single-atom materials
item.description: Multi-principal single-atom materials (MPSAMs) are inspired by the compositional complexity of high-entropy materials and the site-specific control of single-atom catalysis. This perspective conceptualizes key terminology, examines how high-entropy principles shape atomically dispersed designs, and critically assesses strategies to control atomic arrangements. The discussion explores how MPSAMs support cooperative functions across multiple metal sites within a confined space, enabling reactivity and selectivity unattainable with conventional SAMs. Challenges and future outlooks for entropy-informed catalyst design are further outlined.

item.title: Single-chain-water ultrafast transport in COF membrane for dual desalination and devolatilization
item.description: Obtaining clean water requires removing both salt and harmful volatiles—a dual challenge where conventional membranes fall short. This study engineers a synthetic membrane with tailored nanoscale channels that overcome this limitation. It achieves high rejection of salt and volatiles while permitting fast water flow. This is enabled by a unique phenomenon where water molecules line up in a single file to move rapidly through the sub-nanometer pores.

item.title: Advances in polymer chemistry enabled by transition metal catalysis
item.description: Transition metal catalysis has played a central role in driving advances in polymer chemistry. In this perspective, we present case studies where catalytic reactions initially developed for small-molecule substrates were subsequently used for the synthesis or modification of polymers. Applications in the preparation of functional materials and in the degradation, recycling, or upcycling of plastics are described.

item.title: Germanium ligand redox cooperativity: A key to ambiphilicity and switchable two- and four-electron transfer
item.description: This work shows that a main-group compound can be designed to engage in multielectron transfer chemistry often associated with transition metals. By pairing germanium with a redox-active ligand, the molecule can direct either two- or four-electron pathways and display both electron-donating and electron-accepting behavior at one site. This design offers a simple principle for building more versatile, earth-abundant systems for oxygen activation and related transformations in main-group chemistry.

item.title: Visible light steers carbonylation utilizing carbon monoxide toward diversification and practicalization
item.description: This review summarizes recent research progress on carbonylation under visible-light reaction systems. The contents are categorized according to methods for activating substrates. Ultimately, this review aims to inspire the design of novel visible-light-induced carbonylation and promote the advancement of CO utilization in sustainable organic synthesis.

item.title: Cluster-enabled control of single-electron photoredox catalysis in reticular frameworks
item.description: Photoredox catalysis is widely used in solution but remains challenging to implement in solid materials. Here, the authors design the metal-organic framework MUV-1001(Fe) as a self-contained photoredox catalyst by integrating all key functions within its metal cluster. This enables light-driven carbon-carbon bond formation without additives or noble metals. The work establishes a general strategy to translate photoredox chemistry into programmable porous architectures through precise control of cluster composition.

item.title: Emerging trends in light harnessing for CO2 reduction using photocatalytic MOFs
item.description: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are perfect candidates for artificial photosynthesis, yet their wide band gaps often restrict activity to the ultraviolet regime. This perspective explores frontier strategies to overcome this spectral mismatch, focusing on advanced light-harvesting architectures. We evaluate sensitization through plasmonics and quantum dots (QDs) alongside structural engineering of antennae and thin films. By integrating non-linear optical processes like triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA), MOF-based systems can bypass conventional efficiency limits, transforming carbon dioxide (CO2) into sustainable fuels by using the full solar spectrum.

item.title: Operando X-ray spectroscopies for tracking electrocatalytic dynamic interfaces across multiple scales
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Operando X-ray spectroscopies uncover the dynamic catalyst-electrolyte interface across electronic, atomic, and nanoscale regimes, providing mechanistic insight and new strategies for predictive design and durability engineering in heterogeneous electrocatalysis.

item.title: Polymerase-mediated expansion of DNA nanostructures
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

An enzymatic expansion framework for DNA nanostructures is developed in this work. Extendable loops were embedded at the constituent edges of the wireframe DNA lattices to serve as templates for DNA polymerase-driven elongation. Upon enzymatic treatment, controllable unidirectional and multidirectional expansion is realized. Such a controllable expansion not only expands the design space of DNA nanotechnology but also sheds light on expansion microscopy and shape memory materials.

item.title: Site-specific integration of reversibly taggable furylalanine into nonribosomal peptides
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Selective bioconjugation reactions enable important drug delivery strategies, relying on taggable moieties incorporated into bioactive compounds. To address a pressing need for biosynthetic access to reactive, bioactive natural products, a customizable approach to the de novo biosynthesis of Diels-Alder-taggable natural product analogs was established, and its applicability was demonstrated in bioconjugation reactions. The developed biosynthetic platform enables the broader implementation of site-selective modifications in peptide therapeutics.

item.title: Out-of-equilibrium confinement catalysis mediated by compressive force
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Mechanical forces play essential roles in living systems, from hearing and touch to cellular mechanosensing. Inspired by this idea, we show that mechanical force can power supramolecular systems. Applying force distorts a molecular cage and lifts it to a higher-energy state, allowing the guest to escape. Coupled with spontaneous reassembly, this process forms a continuous non-equilibrium cycle. This work introduces mechanical force as a programmable energy input for dissipative supramolecular systems.

item.title: Swarm intelligence for chemical reaction optimization
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

The authors introduce ⍺-PSO, combining swarm intelligence with machine learning for interpretable and automated chemical reaction optimization. By discovering optimal conditions faster than established methods while providing chemists with transparent decision-making, ⍺-PSO enables more efficient chemical process development, accelerating drug manufacturing and sustainable synthesis.

item.title: Array of bimetallic metallophthalocyanine-based metal-organic frameworks for chemiresistive detection and differentiation of toxic gases
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

This work describes the synthesis, characterization, and fundamental investigation of nine octahydroxyl-linked, two-dimensional conductive metal-organic frameworks (cMOFs) based on metallophthalocyanine (MPc). These cMOFs were fabricated into sensor devices, which demonstrated parts per million (ppm)-level sensitivity toward H2S, NO, and CO and machine-learning-assisted differentiation of gaseous analytes.

item.title: Single-molecule FRET enables the detection of site-specific α-synuclein serine phosphorylation
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) combined with phosphorylation-selective labeling enables site-specific detection of protein phosphorylation. Using α-synuclein as a model system, this approach resolves phosphorylation patterns within individual proteoforms with picomolar sensitivity, providing a platform for analyzing heterogeneous posttranslational modifications.

item.title: Single-shot solid-phase synthesis of insulins and their A/B-chain heterodimeric analogs
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Current synthetic approaches for insulin remain labor-intensive and time-consuming. Reported herein is the first single-shot SPPS strategy, which enables enhanced automation and the rapid total synthesis of various insulins and other A/B-chain heterodimeric bioactive peptides in just three steps over 2–3 days.

item.title: Wetting transparency of graphene across length scales: Macroscopic transparency but nanoscopic mirror-like behavior
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Graphene/water interfaces underpin desalination, sensing, energy, and neuromorphic technologies, yet how substrate-supported graphene modulates interfacial water remains unclear. Using surface-specific vibrational spectroscopy and molecular dynamics, we show that graphene is macroscopically transparent but nanoscopically polarizes to counter substrate electrostatics, reorganizing nearby water. This provides new design rules for controlling interfacial water.

item.title: Iridium-mediated methane dehydrogenation and methylidene (=CH2) transfer
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

An iridium complex catalyzes the dehydrogenative coupling of methane and benzene via a methylidene Ir=CH2 species generated through a double methane C–H activation process. A parallel Ir-catalyzed cycle produces formic acid from hydrogen and the carbon dioxide employed as the solvent under supercritical conditions.

item.title: Alcoholysis of nylon 6 waste to ε-caprolactam promoted by phosphoric acid
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Materials made from nylon 6 are widely used but difficult to recycle back into their original monomer, ε-caprolactam. This work introduces a simple acid-catalyzed alcoholysis method that enables efficient and selective depolymerization of nylon 6 into ε-caprolactam. Additionally, this process shows excellent compatibility with a range of real-world nylon 6 materials, including post-consumer fishing net waste, thread, 3D-printing filament, fabric, and carpet, offering a practical pathway toward closed-loop recycling with both environmental and economic benefits.

item.title: Electrochemical reductive carboxylation with carbon dioxide using water as the reductant
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Carboxylation with CO2 provides an efficient method for the synthesis of carboxylic acids. We report here a novel approach that employs water as the reductant for the nickel-catalyzed reductive carboxylation with CO2, which efficiently circumvents the traditionally used stoichiometric amounts of metallic or organic reductants. A divided electrochemical cell equipped with proton exchange membranes was implemented to convert CO2 into complex carboxylic acids in moderate to good yields, coupled with evolution of O2, thus mimicking the process of photosynthesis to a certain degree.

item.title: Oxygen-atom replacement in non-strained cyclic ethers
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

A phosphine-mediated oxygen-atom replacement of non-strained cyclic ethers is reported, enabling rapid assembly of N-, S-, and Se-heterocyclic and carbocyclic molecules. Remarkable functional group compatibility and applications in pharmaceutical synthesis highlight the utility of this strategy in drug discovery.

item.title: Hyperspace mapping and iterative dimensionality reduction reveal radical cascade networks controlled by perovskite-type catalysts
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Robot-assisted experimentation combined with AI-guided dimensionality reduction enabled mapping of the reaction hyperspace and reconstruction of the mechanistic network for cold-start radical cascades catalyzed by previously untested perovskite-like materials, uncovering up to ten discrete—and often synthetically valuable—products.

item.title: Design and organocatalytic enantioselective assembly of axially chiral boracyclohexylidenes and chiral boraspiranes
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

This work addresses two key frontiers: the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of chiral tetracoordinate boron stereocenters to form chiral boraspiranes and the creation of heteroatom-based axially chiral boracyclohexenes. By establishing general methods for accessing these two distinct, previously elusive families of organoboron compounds, we provide versatile chiral building blocks that bridge unique optoelectronic traits with sophisticated architectures, opening new avenues in materials science and asymmetric synthesis.

item.title: A metal-ion-linked self-assembled molecular layer as a robust hole-selective contact for perovskite solar cells
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

A robust and homogeneous metal-ion-linked self-assembled molecular layer (MiLSAM) is fabricated to replace traditional self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) as hole-selective contacts in perovskite solar cells. The perovskite solar cells based on MiLSAM demonstrate excellent efficiency and stability, showing a promising solution to address the challenge of conventional SAMs.

item.title: Trace-water-mediated formamidinium cation anchoring to regulate crystallization of tin-lead perovskite for efficient and stable photovoltaics
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Trace water catalyzes the in situ reaction between benzylamine and formamidinium iodide via a proton-shuttle mechanism, producing BnFA+ to regulate crystallization, suppress Sn2+ oxidation, and reduce defects in Sn–Pb perovskite. The resulting solar cells exceed 24% efficiency with enhanced long-term stability.

item.title: Skeletal editing by iron-catalyzed carbene insertion of trichloromethanes
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

DeMuynck and colleagues describe a new, iron-catalyzed method for carbene insertion of trichloromethanes into a diverse range of indoles. By harnessing commercially available trichloromethane reagents to access iron chlorocarbenes, this simple strategy allows unified access to broad classes of quinolines bearing modifiable functional groups and complex substitutions. Key mechanistic insights are provided for this iron-catalyzed carbene insertion, and late-stage applications of this skeletal editing strategy to peptides and LSD highlight its potential for the discovery of new medicines.

item.title: Out-of-equilibrium sensing with a chemically fueled molecular machine
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Biological adaptive receptors are driven out of equilibrium to change the detectable range of analyte concentrations. Here, a chemically fueled rotaxane information ratchet couples Zn(II) binding to catalytic carbodiimide hydration through an allosterically shifted macrocycle distribution. Because the catalysis sustains a nonequilibrium steady state, the rate of fuel-to-waste conversion reports Zn(II) concentrations at which the same binding site is saturated at equilibrium, thereby widening the range of analyte detection. This principle should generalize to other adaptive supramolecular sensors and signal transduction systems.

item.title: Fabrication of corrugated halogen 2D metal-organic frameworks by means of F···Au coordination
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Halogen atoms are generally discarded in the construction of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) due to their low coordination ability. This study challenges that notion and demonstrates the feasibility of 2D MOF formation on Au(111) via Au···F interactions using fluorinated bowl-shaped molecules. The resulting framework combines unprecedented bonding geometry, non-planar topology, and electronic conjugation. These findings reveal how molecular curvature can reshape bonding at interfaces, offering a novel strategy to design functional 2D materials from underexplored chemical elements.

item.title: Superlattice electrocatalysis matching microbial metabolism for sustainable CO2-to-bioproduct conversion
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

This study demonstrates an integrated electro-microbial system (iEMS) based on a scalable Ag/Cu metal superlattice catalyst. It selectively produces microbe-compatible ethanol from CO2 and efficiently converts ethanol into high-value bioproducts (3-hydroxypropionic acid and single-cell protein), showing an annual profit 15 times higher than that of a single electrocatalytic system. This work highlights the adaptability of the coupling of electrocatalysis and microbial metabolism, paving the way for green development and carbon neutrality.

item.title: Edge engineering of ultrasmall MoSx nanosheets with rich Co sites and S vacancies for polyaromatic hydrogenation
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

We report the in situ synthesis of MoSx nanosheets with one to three layers, lateral sizes of 3–6 nm, and readily cleavable edges with abundant Co sites and S vacancies. The synthesized catalysts rank among the best non-precious metals for the hydrogenation of polyaromatics.

item.title: Solid-state NMR provides location-specific information on the chemical environment inside MOF pores
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

The chemical environment inside MOF pores controls how guest molecules are adsorbed, stored, and transformed within MOFs. We show that 1H and 19F nuclei that are present in the linker or introduced via small reporter molecules can elucidate differences between the chemical environments in different MOF pores. In addition to fundamental insight, solid-state NMR reporters enable facile localization of post-synthetically added ligands, as well as characterization of real-structure effects and the dynamic behavior of node-bound ligands.

item.title: In situ insights from non-equilibrium solution combustion synthesis: From semiconducting thin films to metallic nanostructures
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy of solution combustion reactions reveals the controlled formation of porous nickel metal foams or transparent oxide thin films based on precursor chemistry and reaction geometry. This rapid (≤1 min) and low-temperature technique enables scalable manufacturing of materials for catalysts, perovskite solar devices, and batteries.

item.title: Disentangling the activity-selectivity trade-off in CO2 hydrogenation to methanol
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

For CO2 hydrogenation over Cu-based catalysts, boosting catalytic activity at elevated temperatures drastically compromises methanol selectivity. Herein, Cu chemical properties are tailored via controlled surface coverage, which redirects CO2 adsorption to ZrO2 sites through dual O-atom coordination. This suppresses CO formation from direct C=O bond cleavage at Cu sites, while H2 dissociated on Cu attacks the accessible C center, facilitating methanol synthesis via the formate pathway. This spatial decoupling of active sites effectively overcomes the activity-selectivity trade-off and achieves an excellent methanol yield.

item.title: SAM molecular stacking with heterogeneous orientation for high-performance perovskite photovoltaics
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

This study developed a molecular packing strategy with heterogeneous orientation for self-assembled monolayer (SAM) materials in perovskite photovoltaics. Thermal-evaporated SAM thick films spontaneously form a vertical-to-horizontal gradient in molecular orientation with excellent surface coverage. This heterogeneity gives rise to a gradient energy barrier that optimally facilitates hole transport. The newly proposed strategy is readily applicable for fabricating large-area, uniform SAM films, thereby overcoming a key challenge in achieving homogeneous SAM deposition for scalable production with traditional solution-based techniques.

item.title: DNA-mediated force transmission for precise and efficient mechanochemical activation
item.description:
First article figure (graphical abstract unavailable)

Kim et al. establish DNA as a mechanochemical scaffold, achieving efficient bond scission (99.9% within 15 min) under ultrasound. Sequencing and mass spectrometry enable precise mechanophore characterization, advancing both fundamental mechanochemistry and potential therapeutic applications.
